content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published updated and consolidated guidelines for the programmatic management of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). These guidelines aim to provide a comprehensive framework for identifying, testing, and treating individuals at risk of LTBI, with the goal of reducing the progression to active tuberculosis (TB) disease. The document consolidates previous fragmented recommendations into a single, cohesive set of guidelines to address challenges in implementation and to support national TB programs. Key Highlights of the Guidelines: 1. Definition of LTBI: LTBI is characterized by a persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without clinical evidence of active TB disease. There is no definitive test for LTBI, and its diagnosis relies on indirect methods such as the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). 2. Target Populations for LTBI Testing and Treatment: People Living with HIV (PLHIV): Adults, adolescents, children, and infants living with HIV should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of their degree of immunosuppression or antiretroviral therapy (ART) status. This includes individuals with a positive or unknown TST result and those who have previously been treated for TB. Household Contacts of TB Patients: HIV-negative children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB should receive TB preventive treatment if active TB is ruled out. In low TB incidence countries, systematic testing and treatment for LTBI are recommended for all household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases. In high TB incidence countries, children aged 5 years and older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts may be offered preventive treatment if active TB is excluded. Other At-Risk Groups: Patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, those receiving dialysis, individuals preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, and those with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for LTBI. In low TB incidence settings, testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use illicit drugs. 3. Exclusions from Systematic Testing: Systematic LTBI testing is not recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco use, or low body weight unless they fall into one of the above high-risk categories. 4. Screening Algorithms to Rule Out Active TB: Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment. Chest radiography may be used as an additional tool to rule out active TB in PLHIV, particularly those on ART. 5. Treatment Options for LTBI: The guidelines recommend several treatment regimens, including 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), shorter rifamycin-based regimens, or other options based on local availability and feasibility. 6. Implementation and Monitoring: The guidelines address challenges in implementing LTBI management programs, including resource availability, equity, and feasibility. They also highlight the importance of monitoring and evaluation to assess program impact and improve outcomes. 7. Research Priorities: The guidelines identify areas for further research, including the development of better diagnostic tools for LTBI, cost-effectiveness studies, and strategies to improve adherence to preventive treatment. Development Process: The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary group of experts, including representatives from WHO, national TB programs, academic institutions, and civil society. Seven systematic reviews were conducted to update existing recommendations and formulate new ones. The evidence was evaluated based on quality, benefits, harms, equity, costs, and feasibility. Recommendations Summary: The guidelines include 10 existing recommendations, 7 updated recommendations, and 7 new recommendations. These are categorized according to the cascade of care for LTBI management, including identifying at-risk populations, ruling out active TB, testing for LTBI, providing treatment, and monitoring outcomes. Ethical Considerations: The guidelines emphasize that individual benefit should outweigh risks when recommending LTBI testing and treatment. They also stress the importance of ensuring equitable access to preventive care for vulnerable populations. In conclusion, these updated and consolidated guidelines provide a robust framework for the programmatic management of LTBI, aiming to reduce the global burden of TB by preventing the progression from latent infection to active disease.
